How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming is a 2010 memoir by Mike Brown , the American astronomer most responsible for the reclassification of Pluto from planet to dwarf planet . [ 1 ] [ 2 ]

Summary

[ edit ]
The memoir is an account of the events surrounding the redefinition of the term planet that eventually changed the status of Pluto.

Mike Brown told EarthSky that it wasn’t his goal to kill Pluto. The Caltech astronomer has discovered hundreds of objects in the outer limits of our solar system, but it was his discovery of the dwarf planet Eris that caused International Astronomical Union to demote Pluto from a planet to a dwarf planet in 2006. Brown is the author of How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming . He spoke with EarthSky’s Jorge Salazar.
Pluto was demoted from planet status in 2006, but still, year after year, voices clamor to reinstate Pluto.

But if any one person can be held responsible for Pluto's "death," it's probably Caltech planetary scientist Mike Brown.
Brown led the team that discovered Eris, a frigid world circling the sun far beyond Pluto, in 2005. Eris was initially thought to be larger than Pluto, and the find helped spur astronomers to redefine just what a planet is. Indeed, Brown wrote a book about Pluto's reclassification called "How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming" (Spiegel & Grau, 2010). [ Pluto's Planet Title Defender: Q & A With Alan Stern ]

Two decades later, he still says Pluto had it coming.
by Andrew Moseman
On August 24, 2006, the International Astronomical Union formally reclassified Pluto—our solar system’s then-ninth planet—as a dwarf planet, reducing the planetary count to an even eight.
One of the key players behind that move was Caltech’s Mike Brown, now the Richard and Barbara Rosenberg Professor of Planetary Astronomy and the Terence D. Barr Leadership Chair and director of the Center for Comparative Planetary Evolution. In particular, Brown’s discovery of Eris, an object located near Pluto that is more massive than the former ninth planet, helped set in motion Pluto’s demotion. Despite some popular backlash, Brown would go on to write a book— How I Killed Pluto and Why It Had It Coming —and would adopt “Plutokiller” as his social media handle.
On the anniversary of Pluto’s planetary death this week, Brown authored a retrospective in Scientific American that revisits the questions about Pluto’s planethood, which continue to be debated two decades later. The logical case for the reclassification is as sound as ever, he argues: If Earth’s moon is not a planet, then Pluto isn’t one either. (Because the moon orbits Earth and not the Sun, it fails the first of three criteria for planethood. Pluto meets the first two qualifications: it orbits the sun and is round.
